body:
**PM review — compensating measure delivered, three questions ruled, and one correction I owe.**

## The compensating measure: PASSED

#5018 fired clause ② (published type widened, accept/reject behaviour changed) and ran at opus because fable is exhausted. The price I recorded was a key-by-key check of **declared vs consumed**, hunting one specific failure: a key declared but read by nothing, which re-creates this card's own defect pointing the other way.

The `declared_vs_consumed` table answers it directly — every one of the seven new keys carries a read site (`data` :104/:491, `staticData` :108, `filter` :161/:467, `sort` :468, `map` :199/:217, `enableClustering` :570, `navigation` :554) — and the report states what it deliberately did **not** declare (the flat `latitudeField` / `longitudeField` / `descriptionField` / `zoom` / `center`, modelled in the consumer as `FlatMapConfigKeys` instead). No declared-but-unread key. The failure I was watching for is absent.

## ⚠️ Correction: my ruling was wrong about the `:164` pin

The ruling I recorded on #5018 said the pin at `ObjectMap.filterConfig.test.tsx:164` *"records the OLD precedence"* and *"flips with this ruling"*. I repeated it in the dispatch as a must-not-soften item.

**It is not true.** That test authors no `map` block, so it never pinned a precedence at all — the old top-level-wins order was **unpinned**, and nothing flipped. The seat verified instead of complying, kept the pin, annotated it with what it does and does not cover, and pinned the precedence in both directions in a new test where it belongs.

This is the second time tonight my own ruling text has carried a false premise into a dispatch (the first was #5050's `body` clause). The pattern is the same and worth naming: **a ruling is reused downstream as authority, so a wrong sentence in one propagates into every prompt that quotes it.** The mitigation that worked both times was the seat re-deriving from code rather than trusting the card. That behaviour is correct and I want it to keep happening.

## The second falsified premise is the more interesting one

> a misspelled TOP-LEVEL key is still not a compile error, because `BaseSchema` carries `[key: string]: any` — only the `map` BLOCK is closed

So the fix delivers the card's headline case (`latitudeFieId` inside `map` is now a type error) but **"declare the surface" has a ceiling in this codebase**, and the ceiling is `BaseSchema`. Filed as #5155, correctly as a `finding`.

That matters well beyond this card. There is a family of open cards — #5091, #5097, #5102, #4648 — all of the shape *"the renderer reads keys the declaration denies"*, and all of them implicitly assume declaring the surface makes the wrong spelling unrepresentable. For top-level keys it does not, and cannot, while that index signature stands. Anyone triaging that family should read #5155 first.

## Rulings on the three open questions

**Q1 — keep the flat `locationField` / `titleField` declared? → A, keep them.** Your reasoning is right and decisive: removal is a breaking change to a published type that the ruling never ordered, and `BaseSchema`'s index signature means removal produces **no** type error — so B pays a breaking change for a guarantee it cannot deliver. Both have real read sites, so they satisfy declared-equals-consumed. Documented-as-internal is the correct resting state.

**Q2 — make `ObjectMapConfigSchema` `.strict()`? → A for this PR. I am not ruling B; it goes to the maintainer.** You are right that it is the stronger position and right that it does not belong here. Your framing is the argument I will carry up, because it lands on the dimension that matters most in this codebase:

> a typed-only guarantee protects TypeScript authors and nobody else, and AI-authored metadata is exactly the traffic that arrives untyped

That is agent-error-resistance, and by it B wins clearly. But it changes accept/reject behaviour on a published surface — clause ② — and slipping it in under an alignment card is exactly the move that clause exists to prevent. Filing it as its own card with your reasoning quoted.

**Q3 — should dispatch prompts stop restating the footer? → A.** Already adopted, and you are the second seat to raise it. *"A restated constant is a second place to drift, and this one had already drifted"* is the right generalisation; my prompts will stop restating repo constants that the standing contract owns.

## Two gates that earned their keep

- `check:spec-symbols` refused `MapConfigSchema` because `@objectstack/spec/automation` already exports that name. A real collision caught at the right moment; the rename to `ObjectMapConfig` preserves the ruling's intent (one shared schema) and the ruling's *name* was never the load-bearing part.
- `check:published-dist` caught that a vite string alias matches by **prefix**, so `@object-ui/types/zod` resolved to a directory. Fixed in four configs by ordering the subpath alias first, mirroring the form already pinned in `vitest.config.mts`. That would have been a nasty one to meet later.

And the stop-and-report condition was not merely "not reached" — it was **verified and then pinned**: both flatteners spread `options.map`'s contents flat and emit no `map` key, so the reordered branch is unreachable for their output, and `ObjectView.mapFlatten.test.tsx` now records that rather than leaving it to be re-derived.

Landing once the remaining checks finish — 8 were still in progress at review time, and in this repo my read of every check is the gate.
